title: No Wash, #1! QB House Fit Stations & Opened 760+ Shops｜Curio Archive
description:
You have probably spotted QB House tucked inside a train or subway station—no hair washing, no phone bookings, and just a green, yellow, and red signal light outside. Think cutting hair washing was only about saving ten minutes and utility bills? The real moat rivals could not match was eliminating water and drain pipes—unlocking old stationmaster offices and dead corners right in commuter traffic!
For anyone who has passed a 10-minute barbershop and wondered how a bare-bones model scaled to 767 stores worldwide and over 300 million visits.

This episode starts with an overslept business meeting at a luxury barbershop in the 1990s. See how an industry outsider tested his bold idea in value-conscious Osaka and scored 30% trial interest—six times his goal—then spent three years refining angled seating with scale models. Using ruthless "¥100 per minute" subtraction, he cut phones, umbrella stands, and cash counters, pioneered hair-salon ticket vending machines (installing two per shop inspired by standing soba counters), and added sensor-driven three-color wait lights. Discover how a hanging gas-station nozzle inspired the overhead "Air Washer" hair vacuum, cutting fit-out costs to one-third without floor plumbing and opening the first shop in Kanda Mitoshiro on November 1, 1996. Finally, follow the 3.3-square-meter "QB Shell" pod to Singapore and Hong Kong, Taiwan's 2012 launch and six-month LogiSCut training school, barcode-to-vacuum staffing analytics (averaging 12 minutes 15 seconds), 300 million cumulative visits in Japan in 2024, the February 2025 ¥1,400 price update (opening the ¥100 monthly discount to all ages at the time), and FY2026/6 consolidated revenue of ¥27.15 billion as QB House marks its 30th anniversary across 767 global stores.

This channel has no affiliation or sponsorship with any company or organization mentioned. All timelines, store counts, and financial figures are sourced from the public primary and media references below.

Illustrations in this episode were generated with AI.

q001.text: QB House, a fixture in train stations, cut hair washing to become Japan's top haircut-only chain!

q002.text: No checkout counter, no phone bookings—just a green, yellow, and red light outside.

q003.text: Once the cut is done, an overhead vacuum hose cleans you up, and you're out in about ten minutes!

q004.text: While traditional barbers kept adding washes and massages, QB House stripped them all away.

q005.text: Think skipping the wash only saves time? The real trick is never digging up the floor!

q006.text: With this radical subtraction, it expanded across eight countries to over 760 stores.

q007.text: In Japan alone, it has served hundreds of millions of visits, reshaping the haircut market.

q008.text: Yet when it started in 1996, it was just one tiny shop nobody believed in.

q009.text: Today, let's see how cutting the hair wash let QB House pack barbershops into train stations.

q010.text: This haircut revolution began with a late meeting back in the 1990s.

q011.text: The founder worked in Tokyo leasing clinics and equipment to dentists—a total outsider.

q012.text: Before client meetings, he visited upscale barbershops, spending 4,000 yen and a full hour.

q013.text: Once, he skipped the wash, hot towel, and massage, finished in thirty minutes, and still paid 4,000 yen!

q014.text: Another time, he got the full package, fell asleep under the hot towel, and showed up late to his meeting!

q015.text: Frustrated, he asked himself: why pay for bundled services you never wanted?

q016.text: Looking back, that thirty-minute cut was mostly small talk and touch-ups—the real cutting took ten minutes!

q017.text: So he pitched a wild idea: ten minutes, 1,000 yen, haircut only, no washing!

q018.text: It sounded crazy coming from an outsider—would picky customers actually buy in?

q019.text: Instead of testing in Tokyo, he went to Osaka, famous for value-conscious shoppers, to run surveys.

q020.text: He surveyed bustling Namba, business-heavy Umeda, and suburban Senri New Town.

q021.text: He hoped five percent would try it, but thirty percent said yes—six times his target!

q022.text: He had proof, yet couldn't open: old rules let barber guilds block low prices, stalling him three years.

q023.text: While waiting, his team built scale models to squeeze every single centimeter of space.

q024.text: In narrow shops, they angled two rows of chairs—shrinking the floor space needed,

q025.text: and stopping customers from locking eyes in the opposite mirror! But how do you profit at that price?

q026.text: At full capacity, you earn 100 yen a minute—6,000 yen an hour, beating a 4,000-yen full service!

q027.text: A two-minute phone call loses 200 yen; five minutes hunting for a mixed-up umbrella loses 500.

q028.text: So he cut booking phones and umbrella stands, plus space-hogging magazines and TVs!

q029.text: Coats and umbrellas go straight into each customer's own locker hidden behind the mirror.

q030.text: He even made salon history by bringing in prepay ticket vending machines.

q031.text: Stylists never touch cash or make change—keeping their hands strictly on the scissors.

q032.text: He noticed that when a standing soba shop's ticket machine broke, the whole shop froze.

q033.text: So even in cramped spaces, he installed two machines as backups—never letting sales stop.

q034.text: Remember that three-color light outside? How did it replace phone bookings?

q035.text: Pressure sensors under the waiting bench automatically switch the light based on headcount!

q036.text: Green means no wait, yellow means a short line, and red means fifteen minutes or more!

q037.text: Each station also had a ten-minute hourglass, keeping the pace as tight as a factory line.

q038.text: With everything stripped to the bone, one snag remained: without washing, how do you clear loose hair?

q039.text: Brushing with a towel leaves you itchy all day, yet tiny shops couldn't fit bulky vacuums!

q040.text: The team racked their brains for a year and a half over where to hide the unit and cords.

q041.text: Then he passed a Japanese gas station with overhead hoses, looked up at the nozzles, and cracked it!

q042.text: He hid the motor inside the ceiling and dropped a flexible hose straight down overhead.

q043.text: That created the signature hair vacuum hose, freeing up massive floor space!

q044.text: Tests showed one hose shared by two chairs was clumsy, so every seat got its own.

q045.text: Ditching washbasins and pricey reclining chairs slashed build-out costs to a third!

q046.text: Saving time and build costs was just the surface—skipping floor plumbing was the real killer move!

q047.text: Normal salons must bury water and drain pipes, which railway station floors strictly forbid.

q048.text: And that's not all: he set his sights on old stationmaster offices and storage rooms!

q049.text: These empty rooms had zero plumbing, yet sat directly in the path of daily commuter crowds!

q050.text: Railways could monetize dead space, while QB House got free foot traffic!

q051.text: With the blueprint ready, deregulation finally arrived at the end of 1995!

q052.text: He immediately pitched train stations—only to get turned down flat!

q053.text: Rejected for having no track record, how did he win the railway operators over?

q054.text: In 1996, he rented a street-level shop in Tokyo's Kanda district to let sales do the talking!

q055.text: Even in heavy rain on opening day, it packed out, drawing five TV stations to cover the budget cut.

q056.text: That viral success convinced the railways, and by late 1997 he had twelve shops!

q057.text: After conquering stations, he moved into malls—breaking the men-only image to reach twenty percent women!

q058.text: As stores grew into the hundreds, fewer than one percent ever closed for poor performance!

q059.text: Big profits bred envy, and copycat quick-cut shops flooded the streets!

q060.text: Suppliers even cloned the vacuum hoses, letting rivals buy the whole setup off the shelf.

q061.text: With prime station spots taken and streets packed with clones, where could QB House expand next?

q062.text: It built a 3.3-square-meter cylindrical pod—no renovation, assembled in half a day—for office corners!

q063.text: Could this ultra-compact pod really take off across Japan?

q064.text: Unexpectedly, skipping a waiting area ran straight into Japanese barbershop regulations!

q065.text: Blocked at home, QB House took its pod straight into high-rent malls overseas!

q066.text: It entered Singapore in 2002, then stormed space-starved Hong Kong three years later!

q067.text: Even with triple the rent in Hong Kong, it thrived—and the pod won Japan's Good Design Award!

q068.text: In 2012 it entered Taiwan, also expanding to the US, Canada, and Southeast Asia, with 42 Taiwan stores today.

q069.text: Add 65 stores in Hong Kong, and its global network climbs to 767 stores!

q070.text: Yet going global wasn't enough to outrun domestic copycats: where do you find great stylists?

q071.text: Traditional salons keep apprentices washing hair for years, leaving copycat chains short-staffed.

q072.text: Back in 2012, QB House built its own school to turn master instincts into teachable logic!

q073.text: Even complete beginners can pass the test and hit the floor after six months of intensive training.

q074.text: Because they only cut hair, stylists gain four times the cutting experience of normal salons!

q075.text: It exported that training overseas too, opening schools in Hong Kong, Taipei, and Taichung.

q076.text: And that's not all: skipping hair washing also solved the industry's burnout crisis!

q077.text: No wet hands means no painful eczema, and no bending over sinks makes stylists far more likely to stay!

q078.text: It saves water too: 720 liters per customer a year, totaling over 1.3 billion liters across the chain!

q079.text: Utility bills dropped right alongside, unexpectedly earning a powerhouse eco-friendly reputation.

q080.text: After mastering floor space, water, and talent, QB House still had one final weapon.

q081.text: From the second you buy a ticket, every step feeds into precision data!

q082.text: A timer starts when the ticket barcode is scanned and stops only when the hair vacuum shuts off.

q083.text: With that exact tracking, the average haircut holds steady at twelve minutes and fifteen seconds!

q084.text: Headquarters sees at a glance which stations peak at lunch and which malls surge in the afternoon.

q085.text: Even sharper, it shifts stylists across stores by the hour, shrinking idle downtime to a minimum!

q086.text: In 2017, this system won the Porter Prize, Japan's top award for competitive strategy.

q087.text: The next year, it listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, and customer volume exploded!

q088.text: Then came a new headache: handing out disposable combs for hygiene turned wasteful at that scale!

q089.text: Switching to sterilized combs cut 659 metric tons of CO2 a year—and in 2024, visits topped 300 million!

q090.text: Scale hit a peak, yet rising inflation made the old 1,000-yen price impossible to hold.

q091.text: With prices and wages both climbing, how do you raise rates without losing customers?

q092.text: It actually raised prices gradually from 2014: first to 1,080 yen, then 1,200 yen.

q093.text: Then 1,350 yen in 2023, and 1,400 yen in February 2025.

q094.text: Cleverly, at the time it opened the 100-yen monthly repeat discount—once seniors-only—to all ages!

q095.text: For regulars visiting once a month, it barely felt like a price hike at all!

q096.text: At the same time, it pushed upmarket with new premium shops in Tokyo's Otemachi and Ginza.

q097.text: Adding mobile waitlists and styling finishes unlocked a higher-margin price tier.

q098.text: Beyond price tiers, it even opened nine-to-five short-hour shops to retain parent stylists!

q099.text: What kind of results did all these moves deliver right before its thirtieth birthday?

q100.text: For the fiscal year ending June 2026, revenue surged past 27.1 billion yen!

q101.text: In Nikkei's service industry survey, it even ranked second across all barber and beauty chains!

q102.text: On November 1 that same year, the brand officially celebrated its thirtieth anniversary.

q103.text: Falling asleep in a barbershop chair ended up rewriting everyday haircuts across Asia.

q104.text: Today in Tokyo Station or the Taipei MRT, getting a haircut feels as easy as grabbing a coffee.

q105.text: Yet that's not all: most people completely misunderstand the power of subtraction.

q106.text: People assume subtraction just means cutting corners for rock-bottom prices and razor-thin margins.

q107.text: Truly brilliant subtraction drops outdated habits and rewrites the physical rules!

q108.text: Strip away the hardware assumptions everyone takes for granted, and your territory explodes.

q109.text: While rivals fight a price war in a red ocean, you've already moved to an open track.

q110.text: A clever idea alone will eventually get copied by deeper-pocketed competitors.

q111.text: What built a thirty-year lead wasn't the hardware—it was the discipline behind it.

q112.text: When speed and quality can be replicated reliably, even low prices deliver strong margins!

q113.text: That lesson still cuts sharp today: how many bundled extras are we still paying for?

q114.text: Brands assume more luxury means more value, forgetting that saving people time is worth even more.

q115.text: Slice away every extra step and polish the core to perfection—that's the hardest thing to replace.

q116.text: Next time you pass a station corner and spot that glowing green light on a glass door,

q117.text: remember it's a masterclass in subtraction that rewrote the rules of physical space!

q118.text: Have you ever tried a QB House at a train station? What stood out to you most?

q119.text: Tell us in the comments! And for more business curiosities, subscribe to Curio Archive.
